newsitem.title: CANADA: FOCUS-CP Rail mulls its options for eastern Canada.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-CP Rail mulls its options for eastern Canada.

text.p: Canadian Pacific Railway said on Tuesday it was considering options for its vast eastern Canadian rail network, including its partial or complete sale, or merger with another railway.

CPR Chief Executive Rob Ritchie said in a speech to a railroad group that the company's St. Lawrence & Hudson Railway unit was struggling to make a profit and that a break-even performance was not good enough to survive.
"As the owner, the CPR must consider all of its options for obtaining shareholder value for our eastern assets," Ritchie said.

Calgary, Alberta-based CPR is a wholly owned unit of Canadian Pacific Ltd, the Montreal company once seen as a proxy for the Canadian economy because of its widespread business activities, but which in recent years has divested non-core assets.

St. Lawrence & Hudson was created as a stand-alone unit of CPR in late 1995 to comprise about 3,544 miles of its rail network in eastern Canada and the United States. Of its 3,800 employees, about 600 are in the United States.

St. Lawrence & Hudson lost C$65 million ($48 million) in 1995 and was heading for a break-even 1996, Ritchie said. But he said the turnaround was hampered by low productivity tied to outdated work rules and high Canadian property taxes.
St. Lawrence & Hudson spokesman Terry Liston told Reuters that some Canadian and U.S. short-line rail operators made informal approaches on buying parts of the railway, but he declined to elaborate.

CPR and Canada's other national railway, Canadian National Railway Co of Montreal, have been consolidating their eastern Canadian networks. In contrast to profitable western Canada operations, the eastern Canada rail market has too much capacity and not enough business amid trucking industry competition.
Liston said CPR and Canadian National continued to talk about a possible merger of their networks in eastern Canada.
"Talks cover a range of approaches, including an industry-wide approach in which CN and CP would look at operations across the country," he said.

Analysts said CN would likely benefit most from a merger or rationalization in the eastern Canada rail market because of its dedicated network into the U.S. market through its tunnel between Sarnia, Ontario and Port Huron, Michigan.
They said there was speculation that CPR's eastern Canada network would be sold or merged in a year.
"What has been happening in the eastern Canadian rail market cannot continue. Someone has to walk away," said an analyst who declined to be identified.

CN was Canadian government-owned until November 1995 when it went public in the largest ever single stock issue in Canadian history. Its stock price surged in recent months, reaching a peak of C$57 ($42.40) on the Toronto Stock Exchange in late November.
CN closed down C50 cents (37 cents) at C$52 ($38.30) on Tuesday.
